Neonatal red-necked wallabies (Macropus rufogriseus) emerge after a brief gestation of approximately 27 days [tg = approximately 27 days] at a core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], one of the shortest among the Macropodidae, though older studies such as MercCala1981 report a slightly longer 30-day period. The altricial joey at birth weighs roughly 0.54 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.54 grams], a minuscule mass that underscores the extreme altriciality typical of marsupials. This comparison highlights the remarkably underdeveloped state of the neonate, which must immediately undertake a demanding climb to the pouch to commence continuous suckling. Within the thermal environment of the pouch, also maintained near 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the joey attaches firmly to a teat, beginning an extended phase of milk dependency. The energetic expenditure for the female during this phase is substantial, with the average yearly milk production calculated from growth models approximating 79,780.82 joules per day (approximately 79,780.82 joules per day) , also at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], which reflects the high cost of supporting a rapidly growing pouch young.

Growth within the pouch proceeds steadily, culminating in a permanent pouch exit, which occurs when the juvenile reaches a wet weight of approximately 2300 grams. Weaning itself, however, is not finalized until the young animal attains a significantly larger body mass of 4450 grams [Wwx = 4450 grams] at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], a benchmark that represents nutritional independence from the mother's milk. The period between birth and this milestone of weaning is protracted, typically spanning around 415 days since birth [tx = around 415 days since birth] at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], establishing a long maternal investment period. Some sources, such as Cala1995, indicate a slightly longer duration of 420 days. The juvenile wallaby, now fully weaned, enters a sub-adult phase where it must continue to gain mass and develop the physiological capacity for reproduction, all while foraging independently in its native Tasmanian and Bass Strait island habitats.

The transition to sexual maturity in the red-necked wallaby is a late event in its life cycle, with puberty occurring at approximately 501 days since birth [tp = approximately 501 days since birth] at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. Researchers such as Mayn1976 have proposed a slightly younger age of 450 days, suggesting that environmental conditions can influence the pace of maturation. At this point of sexual maturation, the individual has accumulated considerable body mass, with the wet weight at puberty averaging 6500 grams [Wwp = 6500 grams], indicating that a significant proportion of the ultimate adult size must be achieved before reproductive pathways are activated. Continued somatic growth is necessary even after puberty, as the wallaby is not yet at its full adult dimensions. This delayed investment in growth before heavy reproductive investment aligns with a life-history strategy common among large-bodied macropods, where competition for resources and predation risk shape the timing of first breeding events.

As the individual continues to develop, it eventually approaches its ultimate or asymptotic body size. The maximum adult wet weight recorded for Macropus rufogriseus is 14000 grams [Wwi = 14000 grams], a figure that represents the ceiling for the species' asymptotic mass. Females, typically somewhat smaller than males, often plateau at a lower mass, but the species-wide maximum is robustly reported near this value. This ultimate wet weight (14000 grams) [Wwi = 14000 grams] serves as the baseline for calculating other life-history metrics, including the previously mentioned average yearly milk production. Following the attainment of full adult size, individuals can potentially live for many years. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] at the standard core temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], derived from multiplying 365 days by 10, though very old individuals under optimal captive conditions may occasionally surpass this age. This moderate longevity is coupled with a low reproductive rate, typical of a K-selected strategist.

Regarding annual reproductive output, female red-necked wallabies produce one offspring per reproductive event [N_R_i = one offspring per reproductive event] and approximately 1.28 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.28 litters per year] at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], with a single young being the standard litter size for this macropod. This annual output is constrained by the long period of pouch occupation and the subsequent nutritional demands of lactation. The slow reproductive pace is echoed in the species' social structure, where females often display philopatry and form loose matrilineal associations. The foraging ecology of the red-necked wallaby, which involves selective grazing on grasses and forbs, necessitates a large home range to support metabolic needs. This generalist herbivory, combined with a slow life history, makes the species resilient to moderate habitat disturbance, though it is ultimately sensitive to extreme climatic events and introduced predators.
